title: What hasn't happened yet
title_target: Hva skal du gjøre i sommer?
goal: Talk about the future in three ways that differ in meaning — and avoid the biggest trap for English speakers: thinking *vil* means "will".
bekal: use the present tense for plans with a fixed time
lay out plans for the coming week and year
wave: Review **unit 15** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Name twenty strong verbs with their past forms.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Planer for sommeren
dialogs.intro: Early May. The last snow has vanished from the yard, and suddenly the whole building is talking about July.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Hva skal du gjøre i sommer?
lines.id: What are you doing this summer?
lines.literal: what shall you do in summer?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg reiser hjem til Indonesia i juli. Billetten er allerede kjøpt.
lines.id: I'm going home to Indonesia in July. The ticket's already bought.
lines.literal: I travel home to Indonesia in July. ticket-the is already bought.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Så heldig. Hvor lenge blir du der?
lines.id: Lucky you. How long will you be there?
lines.literal: so lucky. how long become you there?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Seks uker. Jeg kommer tilbake i slutten av august.
lines.id: Six weeks. I'll be back at the end of August.
lines.literal: six weeks. I come back in end-the of August.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da kommer du til å fryse igjen.
lines.literal: then come you to freeze again.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Jeg skal jobbe i juni, og så skal jeg til hytta i juli.
lines.id: I'm working in June, and then I'm going to the cabin.
lines.literal: I shall work in June, and then shall I to cabin-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hele juli på ei hytte? Hva gjør dere der?
lines.id: All of July at a cabin? What do you do there?
lines.literal: whole July on a cabin? what do you there?

lines.text: Ja. Det kommer alltid til å regne. Men vi drar likevel.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Skal jeg bli med neste år?

lines.text: Ja. Men da må du lære å sitte stille i regnet.
lines.id: Sure. But then you'll have to learn to sit still in the rain.

notes: **Norwegian has no special verb form for the future.** What it has is three different ways, and the choice isn't about grammar but about **how certain** it is and **who decides**.

**Jeg reiser hjem i juli** uses the present tense. This is what Norwegians use most for plans that are settled and have a time. English does something similar — "I'm going home in July", "the train leaves at seven".
**Jeg skal jobbe i juni** uses *skal*, which means **intention or agreement**. The subject decides or agrees. This is the most common future form for personal plans — close to English "I'm going to".

**Du kommer til å fryse** uses *kommer til å*, which means **prediction** — something that will happen regardless of anyone's wishes. Weather, age, natural consequences. You don't *decide* to freeze; it's just going to happen.

⚠️ **Vil does not mean "will".** *Jeg vil reise* means "I **want** to go", not "I will go". English speakers use *vil* everywhere because it looks like *will*, and the result sounds like someone constantly announcing their wishes. Think of *vil* as "want to" — like German *will*.
**I slutten av august** means "at the end of August". Its partners are *i begynnelsen av* (at the beginning of) and *midt i* (in the middle of).

grammars.title: Three ways to talk about the future
body: Read the third column carefully — that's where the difference lies.

head: Form
Example
When to use it
rows: settled, fixed time, like a timetable
intention, plan, agreement — the subject decides
something that will happen regardless of anyone's will

after: How to choose in one breath: a **timetable** → present tense. An **intention** → *skal*. A **prediction** → *kommer til å*.

If you use *skal* for the weather, Norwegians will understand but find it odd — as if the rain had signed a contract. The other way round, using *kommer til å* for your own plans sounds as if you have no control over your life.
Norwegian also uses *skal* for movement with no verb at all: *Jeg skal til Bergen* (I'm going to Bergen), *Hvor skal du?* (where are you off to?). This is used all the time.

grammars.title: Word order stays the same
body: The helping verb fills slot two and the main verb goes to slot five — exactly as in the unit 8 rule.
after: Notice that in *kommer til å*, only *kommer* fills slot two; *til å* travels with the main verb to slot five.
The same order works for the *har* form from unit 16 — *har* fills slot two, the third form goes to slot five. One frame, three tenses.

grammars.title: Future time expressions
body: You've been using some of these since units 3 and 11; this table gathers them into one set.
after: ⚠️ *I sommer* can mean "this coming summer" **or** "this past summer", depending on the verb form. *Jeg skal reise i sommer* points ahead; *jeg reiste i sommer* points back. To be completely clear, use *til sommeren* for the one ahead.
*Snart* and *straks* both mean "soon", but *straks* is more urgent — something like "right now".

blocks.text: Future plans come up most when arranging to meet. These sentences can be used exactly as they are.

head: Norsk
English
rows: I may be a little late.

blocks.text: **Jeg gleder meg** literally means "I gladden myself" and means "I'm looking forward to it". English needs a whole phrase for it, and Norwegians use it constantly — for holidays, for the weekend, for this afternoon's cup of coffee.

⚠️ Appointments in Norway are taken literally. *Klokka to* means two o'clock, not ten past two. Arriving five minutes late without letting anyone know is enough to seem rude, and sending a message ahead always solves the problem.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Write your plans for next week in seven sentences, one per day, all with *skal*.
Then write five predictions with *kommer til å* — about the weather, about prices, about what will happen if you keep studying Norwegian ten minutes a day.
Finally, turn five *skal* sentences into the plain present by adding a time expression. Notice that the meaning barely changes — which is why Norwegians often choose the shorter form.
